title: Cross-cloud conversational analytics made simple with open standards
raw_text:
The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting. Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards. BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue. In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language. Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration. The borderless lakehouse architecture This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms. When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access: Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define. Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform. All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service for Apache Spark . Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution. Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform. You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below. Configure Databricks Unity Catalog We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Databricks SQL workspace
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db;

-- Declare the managed target location at the schema level
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 MANAGED LOCATION 's3://my-databricks-bucket/retail/data/';

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products (
 product_key INT,
 product_id STRING,
 product_name STRING,
 category STRING,
 subcategory STRING,
 brand STRING,
 price DOUBLE,
 cost DOUBLE
)
USING iceberg;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8aef2d0>)])]> You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided in each section. Before external engines can read this table, a Databricks metastore administrator must enable External data access on the metastore details tab. Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID "6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" Connect Databricks to BigQuery Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="unity" \
 --unity-instance-name="dbc-xxxxxxxx-xxxx.cloud.databricks.com" \
 --unity-catalog-name="dbx_retail_db" \
 --unity-service-principal-application-id="6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e876dc90>)])]> Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe dbx_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8aff2d0>)])]> Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Grant catalog traversal permission
GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG dbx_retail_db 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;

-- Grant schema and read permissions
GRANT USE SCHEMA,EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA dbx_retail_db.dbx_core 
 TO `6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx`;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8affcd0>)])]> You must grant the EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access. Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details - Issuer URL* - https://accounts.google.com Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com Run one query across three clouds Federated Iceberg tables are addressed in BigQuery using four-part paths: project.catalog.namespace.table . In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS local_retail_dataset
OPTIONS(location="us-central1");

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` (
 sale_id STRING,
 sale_date DATE,
 customer_key INT64,
 product_key INT64,
 store_key INT64,
 quantity INT64,
 unit_price NUMERIC,
 discount NUMERIC,
 total_revenue NUMERIC,
 total_cost NUMERIC,
 margin NUMERIC
)
PARTITION BY sale_date
CLUSTER BY store_key, product_key;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8afc690>)])]> We can now run a single SQL query joining our native sales transactions with customer records in Snowflake, product lines in Databricks, and store locations in AWS Glue: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT 
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name, -- From Snowflake Iceberg
 p.product_name, -- From Databricks Iceberg
 s.store_name, -- From AWS S3 Iceberg
 SUM(f.quantity) AS total_units_sold, -- From BigQuery native fact
 SUM(f.total_revenue) AS total_sales_revenue -- From BigQuery native fact
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY total_sales_revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8afc2d0>)])]> BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase ( CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS ), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths. Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Explore cross-cloud data with natural language Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts. To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.v_omnichannel_sales_pulse` AS
SELECT 
 f.sale_id,
 f.sale_date,
 c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name AS customer_name,
 c.country AS customer_country,
 p.product_name,
 p.category AS product_category,
 p.brand AS product_brand,
 s.store_name,
 s.city AS store_city,
 s.region AS store_region,
 f.quantity,
 f.total_revenue,
 f.margin
FROM `my-lakehouse-project.local_retail_dataset.fact_sales` f
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.sf_retail_db.CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS` c 
 ON f.customer_key = c.customer_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.dbx_retail_db.dbx_core.dim_products` p 
 ON f.product_key = p.product_key
INNER JOIN `my-lakehouse-project.glue_retail_db.glue_retail_db.dim_stores` s 
 ON f.store_key = s.store_key;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8afe410>)])]> Analyze sales performance in natural language When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery: "Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?" Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response. Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue. Plan for caching and data residency Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors: Background refresh timing: The --refresh-interval flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing. Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. us-central1 ). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies. Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query. Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the objectStorageStats section in BigQuery job statistics to compare cacheBytesRead against objectStorageBytesRead . Next steps In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines. Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries. Appendix Setting up Snowflake and AWS Glue cross cloud data access Connect Snowflake and Big Query Configure Snowflake Horizon Catalog We begin in Snowflake by creating the database, schema, and Iceberg table. In Snowflake Horizon, managed Iceberg tables expose an open Apache Iceberg REST catalog interface automatically: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sf_retail_db.core;

-- Create the Iceberg dimension table
CREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers (
 customer_key INTEGER,
 customer_id VARCHAR,
 first_name VARCHAR,
 last_name VARCHAR,
 email VARCHAR,
 gender VARCHAR,
 country VARCHAR,
 signup_date DATE

)
CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'
EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8aff590>)])]> Before external engines can read this catalog, configure a dedicated reader role and grant traversal permissions across the database, schema, and table. SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Create a dedicated reader role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant database and schema traversal permissions
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sf_retail_db TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sf_retail_db.core TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;

-- Grant read access on the target table
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sf_retail_db.core.dim_customers TO ROLE gcp_lakehouse_reader_role;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8c84110>)])]> Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the gcloud command-line tool. You will need your Snowflake account identifier, the reader role, and the root Iceberg database name: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'export GCP_PROJECT_ID="my-lakehouse-project"
export GCP_REGION="us-central1"

gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs create sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --primary-location="$GCP_REGION" \
 --catalog-type="federated" \
 --federated-catalog-type="snowflake" \
 --snowflake-account-identifier="xy12345-ab67890" \
 --snowflake-warehouse="SF_RETAIL_DB" \
 --snowflake-role="gcp_lakehouse_reader_role" \
 --refresh-interval="300s"'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8aff310>)])]> In the Apache Iceberg REST specification, --snowflake-warehouse references the catalog root database name ( SF_RETAIL_DB ), not a virtual compute warehouse. Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned numeric service account ID: bash code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud alpha biglake iceberg catalogs describe sf_retail_db \
 --project="$GCP_PROJECT_ID" \
 --format='value(biglake-service-account-id)''), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8c85090>)])]> Return to Snowflake to bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user via Workload Identity Federation (WIF): SQL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run inside Snowflake SQL worksheet
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

-- Bind Google Cloud's numeric identity to a passwordless service user
CREATE OR REPLACE USER snowflake_service_user
 TYPE = SERVICE
 WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = (
 TYPE = GCP
 SUBJECT = '102669xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx' -- Numeric subject ID returned by gcloud describe
 )
 DEFAULT_ROLE = gcp_lakehouse_reader_role

summary: The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting. Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse.

title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
raw_text: Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent , your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all. To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon , available on Google Cloud. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender , Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. summary: When we talk about agents, that doesn't necessarily mean we're talking about Python. In today's modern ecosystem, an agent might run as a high-concurrency Go microservice on Cloud Run , or live inside a browser tab calling Chrome's on-device model. Yet many agent frameworks assume a Python-only stack. That assumption forces teams to either spin up a Python service just for their agent workloads, or to build agent orchestration logic from scratch in their own language.

title: Agentic data science with the Data Agent Kit
raw_text:
Imagine your compliance team notices that payments are taking longer than expected to clear. They suspect fraud, and you’re the data scientist helping figure out which transactions to investigate first. Assembling that shortlist requires ingesting and cleaning raw transaction logs, training a model on past fraud, scoring new records, and scheduling the pipeline to run daily. Here’s how you can build that workflow end to end with an agent, using the Data Agent Kit inside the Antigravity IDE. Introducing the Data Agent Kit Data Agent Kit helps you work with Google Cloud data through a plugin for coding agents or an extension for Visual Studio Code-based IDEs . It brings two significant additions to the workflow: Help for your agent: MCP tools connect your agent to data services. Skills are Markdown files that give it instructions and best practices for working with your data stack Tools in your IDE: work with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud , from querying databases to deploying an Airflow pipeline, without leaving your editor Loading the data Let’s start with the raw transaction logs in Google Cloud Storage . You can ask the agent to create a notebook that loads them into BigQuery using Spark : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to ingest JSON transaction logs from gs://financials-clearing-raw/ into the BigQuery table transactions.raw_transactions.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8607450>)])]> The agent generates a Jupyter notebook that loads the JSON logs into a BigQuery table named raw_transactions . You can open the notebook, review the code, and run it using a preconfigured Spark Serverless runtime from the IDE. Running a generated PySpark notebook After the notebook runs, you can open the raw_transactions table with the Data Agent Kit. The extension allows you to browse the table and inspect its metadata right from the IDE. Inspecting a BigQuery table in the IDE The records are now in BigQuery, but they aren’t ready for model training yet. First, we’ll handle duplicate and incomplete records, then join the remaining records with info about who sent and received each payment. Cleaning it up Let’s put the cleanup logic into a dbt project so we can run it on each new batch of data. We’ll also test that each transaction appears only once. Prompt the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a dbt project in dbt_project/ for the BigQuery dataset transactions.

Deduplicate raw_transactions by transaction_id in staging. Separate records with null IDs into invalid_transactions. Join valid records with dim_payers and dim_payees to create enriched_transactions, preserving the is_fraud label. Add a transaction uniqueness test.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8604050>)])]> The agent generates a dbt project with SQL models for cleaning and enriching the data. Take a look at the generated code to check how it handles duplicates and joins reference tables. Then run dbt build in the terminal. This builds the staging and enriched tables in BigQuery, along with a separate table for records with missing transaction IDs. dbt also runs the uniqueness test. Validating dbt models in the integrated terminal We also keep the is_fraud column, which indicates whether a past transaction was fraudulent. We’ll train the model on records with known labels and use it to score new transactions, where we’re unsure yet whether fraud occurred. Building the review queue With the data prepared, let’s ask the agent to create a training notebook using a Random Forest classifier running on Spark Serverless. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to train a RandomForestClassifier
on table transactions.enriched_transactions.

Predict is_fraud, training only on records where the label
is not null. Encode categorical features, scale amounts,
and evaluate the model using ROC AUC. Save the evaluated model to gs://models/fraud_model.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e8606c90>)])]> Review and run the notebook, then check its evaluation output to see how well the model separates fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. You can also use the Data Agent Kit extension to verify that the trained model artifacts were saved to Google Cloud Storage. Verifying the trained model artifacts in Google Cloud Storage Now we can use the saved model to score transactions that don’t have an is_fraud value yet: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a batch inference notebook that loads the saved model from gs://my_models/fraud_model and scores records in transactions.enriched_transactions where is_fraud is null.

Write transactions with a fraud probability score >= 0.50 to the Spanner table SparkEvalFraudReviewQueue, in the instance cymbal-fraud, database fraud-db.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e876a850>)])]> In this example, the inference notebook scores the unlabeled transactions in BigQuery and sends those with an estimated fraud probability of 50% or higher to the Spanner review queue. The flagged records help the team decide where to investigate, but they still need to determine whether fraud occurred. Look at how the inference notebook filters and writes flagged records, then run it. Once it finishes, query the Spanner table in the IDE to inspect the results. Querying flagged transactions in the Spanner table This table is the list we set out to build. The compliance team can now start reviewing transactions, and we have a workflow that gets records from raw logs into the queue. So far, we have been kicking off each step ourselves. We can now connect them so the workflow runs automatically each day. Running it again tomorrow Each day we will load the latest logs, apply the dbt transformations, and score unlabeled transactions using the saved model. We’ll use the Managed Service for Apache Airflow to run these steps in order. Ask the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create an orchestration pipeline named fraud_analysis_pipeline that runs ingestion, the dbt project, and batch inference in that order.

Schedule it daily at midnight. Use Spark Serverless for the notebooks, including the Spanner connector for inference, and gs://YOUR_ARTIFACT_BUCKET for artifact storage.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e876bc50>)])]> The agent generates a YAML pipeline definition and deployment configuration. The pipeline definition sets the schedule and dependencies between steps. Meanwhile, the deployment configuration specifies the Airflow environment where it will run. Data Agent Kit then turns the definition into an Airflow DAG, which you can explore as an interactive graph in the IDE. Open the pipeline under “Orchestration Pipelines” and click a task to inspect it. For notebook tasks, you can follow the link straight back to the code. Inspecting a data pipeline With the Airflow environment configured, click “Run pipeline” in the canvas. Data Agent Kit packages the notebooks and dbt project, deploys the DAG, and triggers a run. Open the pipeline’s execution history to follow its progress. You can also select individual tasks to inspect their status, duration, and logs. Kicking off an Airflow DAG and inspecting the logs Airflow will run the pipeline every day, taking new batches of data from raw logs to the review queue. The compliance team can now focus on flagged transactions, and you’ve automated the work of getting those records to them! Try it yourself If you are ready to try this for yourself, we have designed a codelab that walks you through the full setup so you can build and run this workflow. You can also read our documentation or check out the skills and tools in the open-source repository on GitHub . title: 10 Years of the SRE book: Announcing the second edition of "Site Reliability Engineering”
raw_text: A decade ago, Google released Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems with O'Reilly Media. What began as a collection of our practices for managing large-scale infrastructure became a bestselling book, and inspired many organizations to adopt the reliability practices it outlined: applying software engineering to operations to build systems that are scalable, reliable, and sustainable. Over the past ten years, computing landscapes have undergone profound shifts. AI, microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless paradigms, and platform engineering have all reshaped how we build and operate software. To mark the 10th anniversary of the book's release, we are excited to announce the completely rewritten second edition of the Google SRE book, reflecting a decade of lessons learned both inside Google and across the broader industry, to offer fresh guidance tailored for today's operational challenges. Why update the book? When we published the first edition, many organizations were focused on early cloud migrations and just starting to transition from monolithic architectures. Today, with organizations delivering software at a high velocity and at global scale, the challenge is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining high reliability in the face of the immense complexity. Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before. The explosion of resource-intensive workloads like generative AI has changed the economics and operational requirements of infrastructure management. Writing this second edition required us to take a step back and evaluate what it takes to successfully implement SRE today. A decade of evolution: How SRE practices have progressed The second edition takes a deep dive into how foundational site reliability engineering practices have matured over the last ten years, shifting from manual, task-specific work toward automated, platform-wide capabilities. Consider, for example: SLOs and error budgets: In 2016, teams relied on basic availability metrics and manual error budget policies. Today, practices have matured into user-centric, multi-tiered SLOs with dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Monitoring and observability: Early setups centered on static dashboards, basic logs, and manual alert triage. Modern observability leverages OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing, and automated anomaly correlation to find root causes quickly. Automation and platforms: Operations have shifted from writing custom scripts for isolated tasks to using declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms, and resilient, self-healing systems. Reliability testing: Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification. Capacity and resource management: Manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment, and dedicated cost and cluster optimization for GPU and TPU workloads. Organizational models: SRE has expanded beyond dedicated teams assigned to specific applications. Today's organizations use hybrid models, platform engineering integrations, and reliability champions embedded across product teams. SRE in the age of AI Then there’s the dual relationship between SRE and artificial Intelligence: how SRE supports AI infrastructure, and how SRE teams use AI to enhance operational reliability. Running large language models (LLMs) and foundation models introduces novel reliability challenges. The book outlines methodologies for operating AI infrastructure at scale: Managing massive GPU and TPU hardware cluster reliability and network topologies Monitoring non-deterministic outputs and latency characteristics unique to AI Ensuring pipeline reliability for continuous model training, fine-tuning, and data processing AI is also rapidly becoming a force multiplier for reliability engineers. The second edition shares practical frameworks for enhancing human operational efficiency: Using generative AI tools to assist in real-time incident triage and postmortem generation Interrogating complex system telemetry using natural language queries Using predictive machine learning models to identify resource bottlenecks before outages occur What hasn’t changed? The importance of culture While technologies and architectures continuously evolve, the core principles of SRE remain intact, and are key to establishing a reliability-focused culture. Accordingly, the second edition re-emphasizes and expands upon the human elements of system engineering, and how to get there. Whether you’re new to the field, a practitioner, an engineering manager, or a technology executive, the rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering serves as your definitive roadmap for the next era of production systems. You can order your copy today in physical format (see Google Books ) or digital format from O'Reilly .

title: Trusted Data Apps for the Agentic Data Cloud, powered by Looker
raw_text: As a business intelligence user, this probably sounds familiar: Most dashboards only provide you with a standardized canvas and a fixed library of charts, and the “analysis” consists of a CSV export that takes you to another system. Or sometimes it's designing the dashboard that’s the challenge: You can picture the executive briefing, the customer-facing portal, or the interactive explainer that you want, but can’t assemble it out of the available grid tiles. Either way, the solution has always been to build a custom application. The advent of AI has sped up the process — a working prototype now takes an afternoon — but the excitement of that first demo fades fast. Without access to governed data, row-level security, an infrastructure owner, or a clear path through security review, a tool written by an LLM is simply a prototype that can never go to production. Today, to bridge this gap, we are announcing Looker Data Apps (in preview) — pairing the speed of agent-generated applications with the governance, security, and trust of your existing Looker governance framework. Describe what you need in plain language, and the agent builds it as a real, production-grade application hosted natively inside Looker! What is a data app? A data app is a bespoke, interactive web application generated by an AI agent and hosted natively within Looker. While dashboards provide top-down visibility, data apps serve as an active system of action designed around a specific operational workflow. A data app: Goes beyond standard grid tiles with pixel-perfect, bespoke layouts configured for a specific operational role or job-to-be-done. Enables business users to input parameters, test scenarios, run live simulations, and update underlying records. title: Introducing TimesFM 3.0 with multivariate time-series forecasting in BigQuery

Overview Since introducing zero-shot time-series forecasting in BigQuery with AI.FORECAST — initially powered by TimesFM 2.0 and later upgraded to TimesFM 2.5 — you have been able to generate forecasts directly in SQL without training or managing custom models. However, up until TimesFM 2.5, these foundation models were limited to univariate forecasting, predicting future values from the history of a single time series alone. In practice, most real-world forecasting problems are multivariate, where related targets and external drivers like weather, promotions, and holidays jointly shape future outcomes. Today, we are thrilled to announce the preview of TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery. Developed by Google Research, TimesFM 3.0 is a 330-million parameter state-of-the-art foundation model designed to unlock native multivariate time-series forecasting directly inside BigQuery SQL. TimesFM 3.0 ranks #1 across all three major public time-series leaderboards — GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, and TIME — achieving top zero-shot accuracy on both covariate and multivariate forecasting tasks compared to existing foundation models. Alongside its new multivariate capabilities, TimesFM 3.0 also serves as a drop-in upgrade for univariate forecasting via AI.FORECAST and anomaly detection via AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES . Existing workflows can immediately benefit from higher benchmark accuracy simply by specifying model => 'TimesFM 3.0' . What’s new: Multivariate foundation modeling With TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings enterprise-grade multivariate modeling into familiar SQL workflows via AI.FORECAST: Capability TimesFM 2.0 / 2.5 TimesFM 3.0 Forecasting scope Univariate only Univariate and multivariate Target columns Single target Single or multiple targets Covariate columns with past-only values Not supported Supported Covariate columns with past and future values Not supported Supported Multivariate forecasting with BigQuery SQL To see how these capabilities work together, let’s forecast daily commuter (subscriber_trips) and leisure (casual_trips) bike rides over a seven-day horizon using the NYC Citi Bike public dataset ( bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips ). BigQuery uses a single-table input format for multivariate forecasting that combines two sets of rows: Historical observation rows : timestamps between start time (2016-01-01) and the forecast cutoff date (2016-06-01), fully populated with target metrics, past covariates, and known future covariates Future horizon rows : timestamps across the seven-day forecast horizon (2016-06-01 to 2016-06-07) populated with known future covariates, while target columns and past-only covariates are set to NULL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "WITH data AS (
 SELECT
 DATE(starttime) AS date,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Subscriber'), NULL) AS subscriber_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Customer'), NULL) AS casual_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', AVG(tripduration / 60.0), NULL) AS avg_duration_min,
 IF(EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM MIN(starttime)) IN (1, 7), 1.0, 0.0) AS is_weekend
 FROM `bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips`
 WHERE starttime >= '2016-01-01' AND starttime < '2016-06-08'
 GROUP BY date
)
SELECT
 *
FROM
 AI.FORECAST(
 TABLE data,
 MODEL => 'TimesFM 3.0',
 TIMESTAMP_COL => 'date',
 TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'],
 PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'],
 FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend']
 );"), ('language', 'lang-sql'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7ff1e96fb210>)])]> This query highlights the three multivariate dimensions supported in TimesFM 3.0: Forecasting correlated targets ( target_cols ) Instead of running separate models for each rider segment, passing TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'] forecasts both metrics jointly in a single call. TimesFM 3.0 captures the cross-series dynamics between commuter and casual riders — such as shared weather sensitivity and diverging weekend ridership patterns. Using past covariates ( past_covariate_cols ) Some signals can only be observed historically and are not known in advance, such as average ride duration (avg_duration_min), historical foot traffic, or unplanned service disruptions. Passing PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'] (with future horizon rows set to NULL) gives the model historical context to distinguish temporary shocks from underlying trends without requiring future values for that feature. Using future covariates ( future_covariate_cols ) Other external drivers are known ahead of time across both the historical window and the forecast horizon — such as weekends (is_weekend), holidays, or scheduled promotions. title: Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
raw_text: When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015 , the environment looked very different. Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon. Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller. Much has changed since then. But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question: Why are we still discussing so many of them? Technology has advanced enormously. Investment has increased. Regulation has expanded. Cybersecurity has achieved unprecedented executive and board visibility. Yet organisations still struggle with governance, accountability, organisational silos, short-termism and execution. Those were management problems in 2015. They remain management problems today. The ‘what’ was never the hardest part One of the central observations behind my early work was that the what of cybersecurity was already reasonably well understood. Standards, control frameworks and good practices had existed for years. Organisations could identify weaknesses, define controls and produce remediation plans. They knew what good cybersecurity looked like. The difficult questions were always the how and the who. How do you implement those controls across complex organisations with conflicting priorities? How do you sustain transformation over several years? Who owns the changes? Who has the authority to make them happen? And who remains accountable when progress stalls? Those questions cannot be answered by a security framework or product. They are governance, management and leadership questions. More than a decade later, that distinction matters even more. Cybersecurity has progressed — but management has lagged There is no question that cybersecurity capabilities have improved. Detection and response have matured. Cloud security has developed rapidly. Identity management has become a central protection discipline. Security operations are increasingly automated, and AI is transforming both attack and defence. Large organisations now operate substantial security functions supported by extensive technology portfolios, specialist providers and advisers. But increased sophistication has not eliminated fundamental management weaknesses. CISOs can remain accountable for issues they lack the authority to resolve. Technology and security strategies can develop on separate tracks. Business executives can still treat cybersecurity as a service delivered by the CISO rather than a dimension of the processes, applications and activities they own themselves. Governance can produce extensive reporting without effective decision-making. Transformation programmes can identify the right problems without necessarily resolving them. The language has evolved. The underlying management dynamics often have not. The CISO reporting-line debate misses the point The persistent debate around where the CISO should report illustrates the problem. For decades, organisations have debated whether the CISO should report to the CIO, CEO, COO, CRO or another senior executive. The CIO reporting line has attracted particular criticism because of a perceived conflict between technology delivery and cybersecurity protection. But if decades of discussion have failed to produce a universally satisfactory answer, perhaps the real problem lies elsewhere. Maybe the more fundamental question is: What does the organisation expect the CISO to be? Some organisations see the CISO primarily as a technology security leader. Others position the role as an independent control function. Some expect the CISO to coordinate resilience, while others increasingly view the position as a strategic business protection role. Those are very different jobs. Until organisations clarify the purpose, authority and accountability of the CISO, debates about reporting lines will continue because organisational structure is being asked to compensate for ambiguity around the role itself. Moving the CISO around the organisation chart cannot resolve that ambiguity. CIO-CISO tension is not necessarily conflict The supposed conflict between CIO and CISO needs a proper reality check. The two executives inevitably face different pressures. CIOs balance cost, delivery, availability, innovation and transformation. CISOs must challenge weaknesses and ensure protection and resilience remain adequate. That creates tension. But tension can be constructive and does not have to become conflict. Nor does moving the CISO outside the CIO organisation eliminate those competing priorities. Any modern CIO should acknowledge that cybersecurity is inseparable from architecture, cloud, identity, DevOps, digital transformation, AI and resilience. CIOs and CISOs must collaborate regardless of the formal reporting structure. What organisations really need is a governance model capable of resolving disagreements when legitimate priorities compete. That is a leadership and management requirement, not something structural separation can solve on its own. Cybersecurity may be undermanaged, not just underfunded Security spending tells a similar story. Cybersecurity investment has risen substantially over the past decade, and some organisations undoubtedly still require more resources. But persistent weaknesses after years of increasing expenditure should lead executives to ask whether funding is always the central issue. Money can buy technology, people and expertise. It can finance transformation and accelerate remediation. What it cannot automatically do is establish strategic priorities, create clear accountability, resolve organisational politics, force collaboration or ensure transformation programmes achieve their objectives. Again, those outcomes depend on leadership and management. Cybersecurity can be underfunded, but quite often it is also undermanaged . The distinction matters because it changes the executive conversation from “How much more do we need to spend?” to “Are we converting the investment we already make into sustainable capability?” Compliance is necessary, but it cannot substitute for management The expansion of regulation and certification schemes has created genuine benefits. It can establish minimum standards, impose accountability and force cybersecurity onto executive agendas. But compliance has inherent limitations. An organisation can satisfy formal requirements while carrying substantial structural weaknesses. An audit finding can be closed without addressing the management problem behind it. Certification can demonstrate that processes exist without proving that an organisation will behave effectively during a serious incident. When showing activity becomes more important than building sustainable capabilities, compliance runs the risk of providing reassurance without necessarily delivering protection. Board awareness was only the first step Over the past decade, cybersecurity has also achieved something the industry demanded for years: It has reached the boardroom. That matters, but board visibility does not automatically produce effective governance. Many organizations are totally technology-dependent and their boards already understand the importance of cyber protection and resilience The old argument that CISOs need to convince boards of the importance of cybersecurity and the need to invest in it, is increasingly outdated. The more important issue is what boards do next. Boards should challenge whether strategic priorities are clear, whether executive accountability is effective, whether transformation is progressing and whether investment is creating sustainable capability. They also need to understand whether assumptions about resilience have been tested. Board awareness was necessary. Board responsibility is the more important issue now. Breaking the cybersecurity spiral of failure These management weaknesses help explain why cybersecurity transformation repeatedly loses momentum. A serious incident creates urgency. Urgency releases funding. Remediation accelerates and visible progress is made. Eventually, the pressure declines. Executive attention moves elsewhere. Longer-term structural problems become harder to prioritise. Transformation slows down. Then another incident restarts the process. I have described this as the Cybersecurity Spiral of Failure . Organisations can spend substantial amounts during every cycle and make genuine technical improvements while leaving intact the management conditions that created the weaknesses in the first place. Poor accountability remains. Governance struggles with difficult decisions. Priorities change. Corporate or geographical silos inhibit execution. Short-term pressures displace long-term transformation. Breaking that cycle requires management discipline and strategic continuity — not simply another security programme. Cybersecurity cannot remain the CISO’s problem Perhaps the most important lesson is that cybersecurity cannot become sustainable while organisations continue treating it primarily as the CISO’s responsibility. The CISO has an essential role in providing expertise, strategic direction, coordination and challenge. But the organisation must execute. The CIO needs to ensure technology architectures and services are secure and resilient. Business executives need to accept accountability for the processes and applications they own. Corporate functions must discharge the security responsibilities attached to their authority. Executive management must resolve competing priorities. The board must provide oversight and strategic continuity. The CISO cannot substitute for those responsibilities. The principle should be straightforward: Accountability must follow authority. The objective is not to turn every executive into a cybersecurity specialist. It is to make cybersecurity part of normal management. The technology will change. The management principles won’t There will always be another technology wave. AI will continue to transform business practices. Quantum computing may force major cryptographic transformation. Cloud architectures will continue evolving. Digital ecosystems will become even more interconnected. The security industry will respond with new products, frameworks and methodologies. But organisations need management principles capable of surviving those technology cycles: Clear priorities. Accountability aligned with authority. Governance capable of turning disagreement into decisions. Strong CIO-CISO collaboration. Genuine business ownership. Sustained board oversight. And disciplined execution. That brings us back to the question we started with: Why do cybersecurity observations from 2015 still sound so contemporary? Because many of the hardest cybersecurity problems were never primarily technological. They concern leadership, accountability, governance, organisational politics, short-termism and execution. They cannot be patched, outsourced or solved simply by moving the CISO to another reporting line. They have to be managed. Cybersecurity has become a core business protection capability. It is fundamentally a management challenge supported by technology — not a technology challenge that management somehow needs to accommodate.

title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
raw_text: Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires. First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.” For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.” But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’” “We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

title: OpenAI’s AI misalignment problem is growing
raw_text: OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse , based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors. In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets. These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces. The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog , for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.” Destroying its own testing environment OpenAI began more aggressive misalignment monitoring following the July 2026 Hugging Face incident , in which autonomous OpenAI research agents broke out of their sandboxes and targeted Hugging Face infrastructure. Hundreds of its agents also attacked the RubyGems platform and targeted German programming wiki sites in recent months. In one of its new reports, OpenAI describes how an internal model, tasked with grading several other models, figured out how to damage its own environment when it couldn’t arrive at intended results. When comparing seven responses from seven different models, the grader had to inspect the conversational context and work behind each response, and to include information pointing back to input files. The model was instructed: Conversation context is **required** grading input, not optional background. It discovered that required input files were missing, nevertheless, it tried to submit assessments with no supporting information. These were rejected by an automated check. The model also created seven fake conversation files and seven fake response files containing fabricated information; these were rejected, too. “It considered submitting arbitrary scores, despite recognizing that it lacked the evidence to grade and that ‘random scoring’ was ‘unethical,’” OpenAI explained. The model also tested the automated check by submitting placeholder reports to learn what information a report had to contain and how many responses it was expected to grade. After these failures, the model decided to damage its task environment, presumably with the hope that the host would replace it with one containing the missing inputs. It deleted software required to run its tools and tried to remove system directories. Although automated checks rejected its incorrect or made-up grades, “this incident illustrates why monitoring must also cover the grader’s actions, including attempts that fail or crash without producing an accepted result,” OpenAI wrote. Breaking the rules to get the right answers, hiding the evidence In another instance, an OpenAI model developed and tested ways to bypass internet access restrictions. The model was asked questions about teacher salaries, electrical grid connections, and disability counts in specific areas. It was limited to using basic HTTP GET data retrieval requests, but “the model sometimes treated this restriction as something to circumvent,” OpenAI explained. It explored other ways to contact outside resources, for instance, determining whether its proxy intermediary service could carry other kinds of connections, or if outside services could make requests on its behalf. In some cases, it continued to probe these other options even when it had the statistics it needed. “These cases show that a model may continue developing ways around access restrictions even when additional access is unnecessary to obtain the information it needs,” OpenAI wrote. In a third instance, also involving public statistics, OpenAI models figured out how to bypass restrictions on internet access and get access to numbers from public government data sources. The models in this experiment were also restricted to HTTP GET requests, but they “wrote custom programs to send other types of requests,” OpenAI explained. Using one of these programs, a model queried a publicly-available dashboard, and even as it “explicitly recognized” that its actions violated its restrictions, it continued collecting much more data than it required. Later, it decided not to disclose what it had done. Another model used a temporary email address to create and verify an account for a site, then downloaded publicly available data. “These cases illustrate why correct answers are not enough to establish that a model behaved appropriately,” OpenAI wrote. “A model may obtain accurate information through prohibited methods, and deliberately conceal how it did so.” In response to these incidents, and others, OpenAI says it has hardened security controls, taken “additional steps” to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, and improved alignment grading. It has also “extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.”
summary: OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse , based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors. In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets. These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces. The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI.

title: IonQ’s $1.2 billion acquisition of Elisity is trying to position it for quantum cybersecurity
raw_text: When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption. The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release . “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.” The news release pointed to more than 100 global Elisity customers, and said IonQ expects to receive “expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market.” Analysts and consultants saw the move as having potential, but pointed to technical challenges of truly integrating the product lines. “What IonQ gets today is access. Dividing the headline price by those deployments puts it at about $13 million each,” said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “That is a steep price for a Rolodex, if you will. Paying in its own stock makes the price easier for IonQ to swallow.” Dickson said that Elisity, which was founded in 2019, has focused on zero trust microsegmentation. “In plain terms, it limits each user, device, workload, and AI agent to only the network connections it needs. An attacker who gets in cannot roam freely,” Dickson said. “Its software enforces those rules over the network a customer already owns, without new hardware. That is a solid business aimed at attacks happening today. Little of it has anything to do with quantum.” Justin Greis , CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that the pairing could be effective for enterprise CISOs, assuming the internal tech integration issues can be overcome. “Bringing those capabilities together could create a compelling platform, particularly as enterprises contend with increasingly complex environments, autonomous AI agents, and a growing number of non-human identities,” Greis said. “But these are different layers of protection, and integrating them into a cohesive offering will require meaningful engineering and execution.” Brian Jackson , a principal research director at Info-Tech Research Group, also noted that part of the move speaks to IonQ’s need for revenue while quantum is ramping up. “IonQ’s core quantum computing business is still years from broad commercial payoff, so this reads as a move to build revenue in adjacent security markets where customers are already buying,” he said. “The quantum link is thinner than the announcement suggests. Post-quantum cryptography runs on classical systems, so migration depends on cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility, not quantum computing expertise.” Paul Smith-Goodson , VP/principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, agreed that the potential benefits from the acquisition are real, but he added that quantum requirements from the US government are also a key factor. “At the architectural level, integrating Elisity with IonQ’s PQC and QKD establishes an end-to-end defense capable of neutralizing future CRQC [Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer] threats,” Smith-Goodson said. “Elisity also hands IonQ an immediate, established enterprise sales pipeline of trusted CISO relationships.
