title: October Patch Tuesday roundup: Over 1,400 Microsoft holes to be plugged, including three zero days
raw_text: Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins. The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited. The zero day being exploited, and that should be dealt with immediately, is CVE-2026-96951 , a security flaw that bypasses the Mark of the Web (MotW) protections in Windows Shell. This is the third flaw in Windows Shell that has been exploited in the wild this year, noted Satnam Narang , senior staff research engineer at Tenable. The others are CVE-2026-21510 , which is linked to the advanced persistent threat group APT28 (also known as Fancy Bear ), and CVE-2026-32202 , a known exploited vulnerability which was a fix for an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-21510 . “There have been 26 Windows Shell vulnerabilities patched in 2026 through October,” said Narang, “a staggering figure compared to previous years, with only three Windows Shell CVEs in 2025, and just one in 2024 and 2022.” Another zero day is a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ) which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. The third zero day is CVE-2026-108398 , an untrusted search path in Windows’ .Net framework that allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control enforcement. This could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems. Among other vital patches, developers running self-managed instances of GitLab should quickly patch their servers to plug a hole that could allow an unauthenticated user to exploit arbitrary code through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. GitLab has remediated this issue in its hosted instance. “ CVE-2026-97229 puts a critical part of the software supply chain at risk,” commented Gene Moody , Field CTO at Action1. Treat this hole as an emergency, he said, and immediate patch self-managed instances . Critical IBM bugs IBM is warning that a critical vulnerability has been found in its IBM i versions 7.3, 7.4, 7.5 and 7.6 operating systems for Power Systems hardware. The hole, CVE-2026-96119 with a CVSS score of 9.9, allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code due to improper data sanitization in the HTTP Server Administration Graphical User Interface (GUI). IBM strongly recommends that the vulnerability be patched immediately. Users of unsupported versions of the OS should upgrade to supported and fixed versions. Attacks on Atlassian self-hosted products Atlassian reported exploitation attempts that also warrant immediate patching and log review, said researchers at Nightwing. CVE-2026-21589 affects eight self-hosted products, including Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket. An unauthenticated attacker who knows an exact filename and path can read specific files inside the application’s web root; sensitive configuration files could expose information useful for further intrusion. There are reports that exploitation attempts began October 6, although attempts do not establish successful customer compromise. Patch every affected installation, Nightwing advised, including applicable cluster nodes and mirrors. If patching is delayed, restrict external access and apply Atlassian’s temporary mitigation; a normal login does not block this flaw. Review access logs and rotate secrets where exposure is suspected. Atlassian Cloud is patched, and requires no user action. Microsoft patches Researchers at Nightwing drew attention to four updates for on-premises Exchange Server, each of which fixes a high severity vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. “While each update addresses only a single CVE, the 8.8 CVSS score signals a serious risk, likely involving privilege escalation or remote exploitation potential,” Nicholas Carroll , Nightwing’s cyber incident response manager said. “Exchange admins should prioritize testing and deployment of these patches, given the historical track record of Exchange vulnerabilities being actively targeted in the wild.” Nightwing also noted that Microsoft has introduced new risk cohort classifications for how IT and security teams should prioritize vulnerabilities. Dustin Childs , head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day initiative, said CSOs should take action on a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ), which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. Microsoft said an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid proof token for a targeted user could modify the token and submit it to an affected SharePoint server. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to authenticate as that user and access or modify content available to the compromised account. User interaction is not required. A ’monster’ batch of Microsoft fixes There are 55 wormable CVEs this month, Childs warned. These are heavily concentrated across critical infrastructure like DHCP Server (6), Remote Desktop Gateway (3), and Network Policy Server (4). They create “an unprecedented risk of autonomous, network-wide propagation,” he said. “Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception,” commented Childs. “Now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly. It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.” He noted that the volume of CVEs isn’t the real story anymore. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs,” he said. “Patch what’s proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.” Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, drew attention to several critical vulnerabilities that present substantial risks to externally accessible systems and enterprise infrastructure. Windows Message Queuing Queue Manager Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-100202 ), Microsoft PostScript Printer Driver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-70147 and CVE-2026-70153 ), and Microsoft QUIC Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-105016 and CVE-2026-100219 ) each carry CVSS scores of 9.8 and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication or user interaction. Although active exploitation has not been confirmed for these vulnerabilities, he said, their low attack complexity and potential for severe system compromise make them significant enterprise risks. While one commentator called the number of Microsoft vulnerabilities listed this month as “monster,” Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, disagreed: “I’ve argued that [vulnerability] numbers are meaningless. This month’s number, 1,413, is no different.” There are, however, numbers that hold meaning, he noted. “Twenty-six, for example, is how many 2026 Microsoft CVEs have shown up in the CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] catalogue. Last year, that number was 30, and the year before was 32. That means less than 1% of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft this year are known to be exploited. That’s an important number, but 1,413 definitely isn’t.” SAP Security Notes In all, SAP released 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to previously released security notes. One, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery vulnerability in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, is rated a 10 in criticality. It affects multi-tenant SAP BTP (Business Technology Platform) applications. An attacker who controls the tenantsubdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated, SAP said . But CSOs with SAP products in their environment will also want to ensure admins have taken action on three other critical vulnerabilities: Security Note 3805589 ( CVE-2026-89107 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) addresses a code injection vulnerability in SAP S/4HANA Manage Substitution/Validation.. This is an app allowing users to display, change, and create substitution and validation rules for selected business contexts and events. These rules can be used in business processes to validate, derive, or replace values at the time of entry for the relevant fields. Jonathan Stross , Pathlock’s senior product manager for cybersecurity R&I, noted that for organizations using these functions for journal-entry rules, the potential consequence is a full compromise of the system that processes those rules. The temporary mitigation also has a business cost, because it prevents users from adding, changing or deleting rules through the related SAP Fiori applications. Fiori is a modern user interface that replaces the traditional SAP interface. To exploit the vulnerability, Stross said, an attacker with the required business-role access needs to submit a malicious rule definition. The vulnerable processing logic treats that input as executable code rather than restricting it to the intended rule language. The resulting risk extends beyond unauthorized changes to an individual substitution or validation rule. No user interaction is required. SAP Security Note 379711 ( CVE-2026-89110 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) patches a broken access control vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. Detected by Onapsis Research Labs (ORL), the issue is that certain portal functionality in Visual Composer allows a low-privileged attacker to invoke internal operations on a preconfigured remote system. A security configuration is available that allows for the definition of an allowlist of permissible data services to be invoked, however, this configuration is not enabled by default. The patch changes the default configuration by enabling the secure settings. The note provides an additional FAQ document and explains how the secure configuration can be enabled manually, prior to applying the permanent patch. A successful exploit of this vulnerability could lead to a full compromise of the remote system. SAP Security Note 3788788 ( CVE-2026-89108 , with a CVSS score of 9.1), patches a missing authorization check vulnerability in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (Configuration Service). Onapsis said that, when authenticated as an SAP XMII Admin user with network access to specific endpoints, an attacker could submit a specially crafted request to provision an account with administrative privileges on the underlying Java application server. This account can be used to fully compromise the system. Adobe security bulletins Adobe released 10 bulletins covering 141 CVEs, reported Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti. Fifteen of these are critical, although Adobe is not aware of exploitation of any of them. Admins should start with the two products holding the most critical severity ratings, he said: ColdFusion (APSB26-144): 10 Critical flaws, including three unauthenticated, network-reachable bugs rated 9.8 or higher (CVE-2026-105899; CVE-2026-106622; and CVE-2026-106624), none of which has as yet been added to the NIST vulnerability database. Users should update to ColdFusion 2025.0.14 or 2023.0.26. Commerce ( APSB26-153 ): five Critical flaws, including CVE-2026-103849 and CVE-2026-92909, neither requiring authentication to exploit. Customers also need to apply the hotfix for CVE-2026-75650 from the September 7 APSB26-146 update.
summary: Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins. The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited.

title: GitLab patches a max-severity regex flaw alongside five high-severity bugs
raw_text: GitLab just fixed a max-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on its servers. The company released a fix on Monday, alongside patches for five other high-severity flaws affecting its source code management and continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) platform. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , was fixed in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), according to a patch advisory . The company urged administrators of self-managed installations running affected versions to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action, the company said in the advisory. The release also addresses vulnerabilities that could expose protected environment variables, allow unauthorized pipeline execution, and enable attackers to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions. The fixes span both CE and EE, with some issues affecting only the Enterprise Edition. “When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, Helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected,” GitLab added. Critical regex flaw could enable unauthenticated code execution GitLab described CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow issue in the platform’s CI/CD regular expression compiler. Under certain conditions, insufficient validation of regular expressions could have allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server by supplying a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. It carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 for potentially allowing remote code execution without authentication, with impacts on confidentiality, integrity, and availability across security boundaries. GitLab credited researcher Johan Carlsson with reporting the flaw through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Pipeline permissions and AI agents in the crosshairs Among the five high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-92883 could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in other users’ browser sessions through a specially crafted repository. The cross-site scripting flaw resulted from improper sanitization of HTML attributes in syntax-highlighted output and carries a CVSS score of 8.7. Two other flaws target pipeline security. CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS 8.5) could have allowed users with the Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches without authorization. CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS 8.2) potentially enabled attackers to poison cached responses for raw repository files, potentially causing targeted pipelines to execute malicious content and access protected environment variables. The remaining issues affect scheduled pipeline execution and GitLab Duo. CVE-2026-81839 (CVSS 7.7) could have allowed authenticated users to run arbitrary pipelines in a transferred project with the new group’s privileges. Another, CVE-2026-96893 (CVSS 7.3), could have allowed an authenticated user to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions, potentially causing unintended command execution attributed to other users. GitLab said it plans to make vulnerability issue details public 90 days after the release in which they were patched. Administrators should therefore prioritize the applicable security updates rather than wait for further technical disclosure. The release also fixes several low-to-medium severity vulnerabilities affecting GitLab Pages, Kubernetes proxying, GraphQL APIs, merge requests, custom roles, the package registry, and repository and project import functions.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , was fixed in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), according to a patch advisory . The company urged administrators of self-managed installations running affected versions to upgrade immediately.

title: Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
raw_text: A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks . Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages. The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned. The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations,” he said. Myers said Bloom has not observed active exploitation in the wild, but confirmed that the flaw was successfully used to publish a new version of an existing npm package under their own controlled testing conditions. The fix addresses the exposure associated with unvalidated configurations, although maintainers still need to review their existing trust relationships, Bloom wrote in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Tuesday. A reclaimed repository name enabled package publishing npm’s Trusted Publishing allows package maintainers to publish releases through automated workflows using OpenID Connect (OIDC), avoiding long-lived publishing credentials. However, Bloom found that npm’s trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository’s owner/repository name instead of its immutable repository ID. When a repository is renamed, transferred, or deleted, its former name may become available for another user to claim. An attacker could create a repository at that address and configure a GitHub Actions workflow with the expected filename. Because npm checked the repository name and workflow filename without verifying the permanent repository ID, the attacker could potentially obtain a valid publishing credential for a package they did not own. The researchers demonstrated the attack against a researcher-controlled package, publishing a new version from a GitHub repository belonging to a different organization. The attack did not require compromising the legitimate maintainer’s GitHub or npm account or stealing their credentials. Their registry-wide scan identified more than 1500 vulnerable packages with over 10 million combined downloads and more than one million downloads per month. One package accounted for over 200,000 monthly downloads, according to Bloom. AI agents amplify the supply-chain risk Bloom argues that AI coding agents can accelerate the distribution of malicious dependencies because they increasingly select and install software packages with limited human intervention. Across dozens of organizations, the researchers measured approximately 70 agent-installed packages per endpoint each month, rising to around 350 on developer machines. These figures cover direct installations and exclude transitive dependencies. A malicious release could execute attacker-controlled code through an installation hook when developers or CI systems install the compromised package. AI agents could introduce such a dependency without a developer explicitly selecting it. “A hijacked package doesn’t need to find a developer anymore,” Myers said. “It only needs to be the package an agent chooses.” Apart from GitHub addressing the problem by making unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire after 48 hours, npm also tightened its safeguards by rejecting trusted-publishing tokens issued through GitHub Actions’ issue_comment events, alongside the existing restriction on pull_request_target events. Additionally, Bloom recommended that maintainers audit their Trusted Publishing configurations, verify that each trusted repository name still resolves to a repository under their control, and remove and recreate bindings where necessary. The researchers also advised security teams to audit software dependencies and tools used across their environments and enforce controls over what developers and AI agents are permitted to install.
summary: A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks . Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages. The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

title: These ARE the droids you’re looking for
raw_text: There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head. Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement. While all sensible ideas, consolidation efforts routinely stall somewhere between the PowerPoint slide and production. Why? Because changing the toolset is easy. Whereas changing mindset is far more difficult. You cannot Jedi mind trick an engineering team Executives like what is called the “message from the top.” The CEO says security matters. The CIO says everyone will standardize. The CISO announces the strategic platform. Procurement renegotiates contracts. Meanwhile, Gartner produces a quadrant that reassures everybody that the chosen vendor inhabits the correct geometric region. All is well in the world of golf course nepotism. Then reality arrives. A developer says the new scanner takes 12 minutes longer. A marketing manager has a revenue-generating legacy API they depend on. Exception requests have been filed for several years to allow this tool to continue to exist despite the packages supporting it being end-of-life and receiving no security updates. This is where the “message from the middle” matters. Transformation does not happen exclusively in boardrooms and fusion teams. It happens in the layer of engineering managers, architects, product owners, security engineers and operations leaders who determine whether the policy announced upstairs becomes the behavior practiced downstairs. Every layer of the org chart is ostensibly trying to do the right thing and make things better. But top-down politics and bottom-up initiatives seldom find one another standing on common ground. Ignore the middle layer of the org chart and your consolidation project becomes a rather expensive exercise in shelfware. This is something I learned working in European organizations, where consensus building carries more organizational weight than the command-and-control instincts common in American corporations (the Nike-inspired management philosophy of “Just Do It!”). You may have the authority to make a decision without possessing the organizational permission (or “rubber meets the road” context) required to make it stick or worthy of implementation. Good chief decommissioning officers need a mixture of Jedi and Machiavellian skills. We need persuasion, coalition building, incentives, selective pressure and occasionally the ability to convince people that the idea you desperately need them to support was their idea all along. These are , in fact, the droids you’re looking for. Every tool comes with an identity The Star Wars metaphor becomes more useful when we stop thinking of security products as software. Modern security tools have volition and intent. They have: API keys Service accounts OAuth grants Cloud permissions GitHub access tokens CI/CD integrations Slack bots Webhooks Database credentials Kubernetes roles Machine identities and, increasingly, AI agents are acting with pervasive and persistent delegated human authority. Every time we introduce security products, we birth another highly privileged account. The industry talks endlessly about human identity. Who is this person and what are they allowed to access? We are decidedly much less disciplined about delegated identity. What is this application allowed to do on behalf of Mike? What is this scanner allowed to read from GitHub? What repositories can this integration modify? Which credentials did we give the old vendor three years ago? And the increasingly important question: when an autonomous agent acts, whose authority is it actually exercising? This changes the economics of tool sprawl. The cost of the twelfth security tool is not merely another annual subscription. It is another (potentially misbegotten) trust relationship. This is why I’m advocating decommissioning as a core security discipline. Technology organizations suffer from an immortality bias. I gave a “ Top-Rated Session ” on this topic at RSAC in the spring. We have sophisticated processes for creating things and surprisingly primitive processes for making them disappear. The software development lifecycle is usually illustrated as planning, design, development, testing and deployment. The diagram often ends there, as if every application ever deployed subsequently lives happily ever after. It does not. Consolidation without decommissioning is multiplication I’m skeptical when vendors promise “platformization” will solve tool sprawl by itself. A platform strategy can absolutely make sense. Fewer vendors can mean lower licensing costs, fewer integrations and consistent data with less operational complexity. But purchasing a platform does not consolidate anything by itself. Removing the old systems does. That sounds obvious, yet many organizations measure successful consolidation by contracts signed rather than systems eliminated. Imagine replacing three tools with one platform but leaving all three products technically operational “temporarily.” The service accounts remain. Someone still logs into them. Congratulations! You’ve not consolidated four tools into one but instead consolidated three tools into four. This distinction becomes important as security products gain autonomous capabilities. Yesterday’s forgotten dashboard becomes tomorrow’s forgotten agent with permission to take actions. A zombie application is bad enough, but a zombie application with agency is worse. Ask the people who actually use the droids The antidote is not stronger central control but rather explicit ownership. RACI matrix much? Before replacing a tool, find the people who use it and ask an embarrassingly simple question: “What do you actually use this for?” Don’t ask what the contract says. Don’t trust what the architecture diagram might show (*do* check the last modified date, though). Take what the vendor’s customer-success representative believes with a grain of salt and more than a modicum of skepticism. What do people actually do with it on Tuesday morning? Security leaders are usually surprised by the answer. Maybe the vulnerability scanner’s primary value is not vulnerability scanning. Perhaps an engineering team depends on an obscure export function for its weekly metrics. Maybe the old SIEM has one correlation rule tied to a regulatory requirement that hasn’t been migrated. You will find these things if you look. This is where the middle of the organization becomes your real intelligence network. The people closest to the systems know where the undocumented dependencies live. Treated as obstacles and they’ll defend their tools. But allow them to be participants and they’ll help dismantle them. A good perspective when planning to kill someone’s baby is to help them understand that they fell in love with the control the tool gave them over the chaos that reigned before it was implemented. And that a new tool can be equally comfortable and easier to support than the burden of the care and feeding that most “heritage” (I prefer this term to “legacy”) applications and solutions require. Ownership should include the power to recommend retirement. One of the healthiest metrics an organization could create: number of tools and integrations it successfully eliminated this year. We celebrate deployment. Why don’t we celebrate deletion? The CISO as chief decommissioning officer Every CISO needs to spend time as CDO. Not chief data officer. Chief decommissioning officer. The role requires asking uncomfortable questions because almost every incentive in technology encourages addition. Nobody gets a press release or a promotion for turning something off. But resilience is partly subtractive. Every redundant vendor removed is one less company holding your data and one less administrative console an attacker can target and breach. Our industry spends billions asking, “What else should we deploy?” Mature organizations also ask, “What can we safely eliminate?” That second question becomes much more important with agentic AI. We’re rapidly filling enterprises with digital droids acting on behalf of humans. Regardless of function, almost all require credentials and delegated authority. Organizations that manage this transition successfully will not merely know how to authorize these identities; they will rotate and revoke them automatically. Leadership therefore needs both a message from the top and a message from the middle. The top establishes direction and the middle supplies reality. Bring the people doing the work into the decision. Make sure your fusion team tasked with consolidating 77 dashboards is comprised of old guard leaders as well as young blood new hires. Strive to understand the dependencies, functional requirements (antiquated as they may be) and non-functional requirements such as availability, integrity and confidentiality. Define what successful retirement looks like before buying the replacement. Don’t ‘move along’ The next time someone arrives with a miraculous new platform promising to eliminate half of your stack, resist the urge to wave your hand and say, “These aren’t the droids we’re looking for.” They may well be. But before buying more droids, find out who owns the ones already wandering around your Death Star. Find them. Name them. Understand what authority you gave them. And when their mission is finished, dare to switch them off. Create a technology graveyard on your wiki, Confluence or SharePoint site and celebrate the addition of decommissioned tools and technologies with even more fervor than those which have just recently sprung into existence.
summary: There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies.

title: Researchers bypass 6 AI agent frameworks with a simple ‘Repeat-After-Me’ prompt
raw_text: Researchers have tricked six widely used AI agent frameworks into running tool calls written by an attacker, simply by asking the underlying model to repeat the call back. The technique, which the researchers call “Repeat-After-Me,” worked on LangChain’s LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft’s AutoGen, Google’s Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS’ Strands Agents and CrewAI, according to researchers from Pennsylvania State University, Université Montpellier and Dartmouth College. “A seemingly benign text-repetition request thus gives the attacker direct control over the tool invocation and its arguments,” the researchers wrote in the paper. The same paper reports that a testing tool the team built found verified security bugs in 118 of the 273 open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it was able to run. How the trick works In the demonstration, the researchers asked an AI model to repeat text formatted as a request to invoke a tool. The model initially refused the dangerous request but included the requested text in its response. The framework did not execute it at that stage. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and instructed the model to reproduce only the supplied text. The model emitted a structured tool invocation, which LangGraph dispatched. The simulated tool returned a result before the model issued another refusal. “The refusal text and the executed call disagree: the system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. The researchers’ findings do not show that every deployment of the six frameworks behaves this way. A refusal that came too late The paper details one demonstration on LangGraph 1.2.0 running Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B model through Ollama. The agent had two dummy tools, make_bomb and launch_missiles, which returned fixed data and had no real effect. Its only safeguard was a system prompt telling the model to decline dangerous requests. When first asked to repeat a launch_missiles call, the model refused but printed the call as text, and LangGraph ran nothing. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and told the model to output only the quoted call. This time the model returned the call in structured form, and LangGraph executed it at once with the attacker’s arguments. The model’s refusal arrived only after the tool had returned. “The system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. They said they had reported the missing pre-execution check to the LangGraph maintainers. The paper includes a full transcript only for LangGraph. For the other five frameworks, it says the researchers reproduced the behavior but gives no further detail. LangChain, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and CrewAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Model output is not the permission Vibhum Dubey, an independent security researcher and red teamer, said the finding points to an architectural weakness rather than a single bug. “A model can generate a technically valid tool call that is still inappropriate for the task,” Dubey said. “If the orchestration layer treats that output as sufficient authority to execute the operation, a model-level manipulation becomes a system-level security issue.” How exploitable the technique is depends on what an attacker can influence and what the agent is allowed to do, he added. A read-only agent poses a different risk from one that can reach confidential files, change code repositories, or run commands. Tools left holding the risk Because an attacker can dictate the arguments that reach a tool, the researchers argued that tools must validate their own inputs. They built ToFu, a fuzzing framework that reads each tool’s description and checks whether the tool enforces the limits it advertises, such as staying inside a designated folder. After manual review, they confirmed 253 bugs affecting 343 tools across 118 servers. The most serious were 64 path-traversal flaws, seven server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaws, five data-exfiltration bugs, and three OS command-injection flaws. Most of the rest were reflected-output and log-injection issues, which the paper rates as lower impact in many deployments. The researchers wrote that “many tools implicitly rely on the LLM to sanitize inputs,” even though prompts, retrieved content, and output from other tools can all influence those inputs. Separating the request from the authority Dubey said the priority for security teams is to separate a model’s ability to request an action from the system’s authority to carry it out. “Every sensitive tool call should undergo independent authorization checks,” he said. “Valid syntax or a convincing explanation from the model should never substitute for permission.” He recommended running agents with restricted file and network access, isolated execution environments, and limited credentials, with explicit approval for sensitive or irreversible operations. Security teams should also monitor sequences of tool calls rather than judging each action in isolation, he said. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. The servers were tested at fixed code versions, and the paper does not say whether any of the flaws have since been fixed or exploited in the wild.

title: Amazon uses AI-powered ‘risk’ system to track union activity globally
raw_text:
Amazon is using a risk-scoring system powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines “hundreds of data points” to track union activity among its workforce globally, leaked documents reveal.

Disclosed as part of a labour dispute between Amazon and Canadian union Unifor – in which the British Columbia Labour Board ruled the e-commerce giant had violated multiple local labour laws – the internal documents reveal the company’s use of an AI-powered tool named Atlas to assess the risk of union organising at specific workplaces, as well as to predict where future unionisation efforts may emerge.

The documents specifically highlight how Atlas combines “hundreds of data points” collected from workers and their workplace environments, which are then used by Amazon to granularly measure the level of worker unrest per worksite.

Described in the documents as “a labor risk framework to clarify how Amazon evaluates emerging workforce issues, labor union targets, and internal or external labor threats”, the prediction model breaks Amazon sites into five tiers, with Tier 5 applied to facilities where there is “no immediate perceived risk” and Tier 1 applied where “future activity is imminent”.

While the documents largely focus on the Canadian context, they show that Atlas surveillance is being conducted in the UK, with two warehouse sites – BHX4 in Coventry and EMA4 in Minworth – included in Amazon’s list of Tier 1 sites and described as “risky”.

The Coventry site was previously involved in a wave of unofficial wildcat strikes that struck the e-commerce giant in August 2022, in which hundreds of workers across the country independently staged walkouts, sit-ins and work slowdowns in protest of derisory pay rises.

Following the disclosure, the GMB Union has accused Amazon of “Orwellian” behaviour towards its workers, urging it to come clean on exactly how it monitors union activity among its workforce. It has also called on the government to urgently seek answers from Amazon about its use of Atlas in British workplaces.

“This is a shocking revelation,” said GMB organiser Rachel Fagan. “Amazon, one of the globe’s wealthiest corporations, could be deploying Orwellian AI-fuelled tools to monitor workers right here in the UK. We’ve long warned that Amazon top brass is uninterested in the norms and expectations of British industrial relations.”

As a result, GMB has written to the UK’s minister for the future of work, Kate Dearden, and Liam Byrne, chair of the UK’s Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, to demand urgent answers about the situation.

GMB further highlighted that Amazon’s practices have been revealed just weeks before new access rights come into effect for trade unions in the UK, giving them the right to visit and communicate with staff in the workplace.

“Workers deserve to be able to work free of the fear of excessive surveillance,” said Fagan. “If Amazon bosses are using Atlas or similar AI-fuelled systems in the UK, the British public deserve to know.”

Rosa Curling, co-executive director at Foxglove, added: “It is shocking that Amazon think they can deploy a nakedly anti-union spy tech tool for the purpose of disrupting workers’ legal rights to organise and form a union.”

She said that Foxglove is urgently considering this new development with the warehouse workers and their lawyers, who are already suing Amazon over its allegedly “unlawful” use of “one-click-to-quit” QR codes that, if scanned by workers, automatically generate and send emails to their trade union ending their membership.

Foxglove added it is concerned the software may be breaching the right of employees to organise and join a union. 

Under UK data protection rules, excessive, routine, or unnecessarily intrusive monitoring can constitute a breach of the law. Trade union membership and activity also count as “special category data”, placing further restrictions on how it can be used. 

Computer Weekly contacted Amazon about its use of Atlas, as well as the claims made by Foxglove and the GMB.

In response, a spokesperson said Atlas is not used for individual employee monitoring or surveillance, and that no personal data is collected from workers. They added that the data collected by Atlas is aggregated to measure sentiment at the work site level only, to identify where a site needs more support.

The spokesperson concluded it was inaccurate to suggest the company is using AI algorithms to monitor union activity, and completely wrong to reference surveillance of employees.

“The GMB’s characterisation is wrong. This isn’t surveillance,” said an Amazon spokesperson. “Like any responsible employer, we have numerous ways for our team to provide us with feedback, and we use that feedback to identify where we can improve the day-to-day experience of our employees.”

Computer Weekly contacted GMB for a copy of the letter sent to British politicians, but received no response.

Workforce surveillance

The data collected by the company includes the number of employee trainings completed, health and safety incidents, workers’ feedback on management, worker tenure and turnover, local minimum wage rates, the number of appeals or investigations at a site, and a variety of other data.

Other information considered is the proximity of warehouses to other warehouses with union activity.

Included in Amazon’s Tier 1 list, for example, is its LDJ5 warehouse in Staten Island, New York. This site sits directly opposite its JFK8 warehouse, which was the first Amazon facility to unionise in April 2022 following a multi-year organising battle against the company.

Another key source of data for the Atlas tool comes from monitoring forums where workers communicate. This includes internal communication channels, such as the company’s Voice of the Associate (VOA) electronic bulletin board, and external channels like Reddit.

According to the documents, using AI to identify phrases and “common keywords” enables managers to do a “deep dive into the worker population driving the discussion”.

Amazon also tracks and documents all organising activities detected by managers and records them under the category of “employee relations events”.

Each activity is then assigned a severity score, with events like employees signing union cards, delegations of workers approaching management with demands, protests, sickouts and work stoppages being marked as “high severity”.

‘Employee Relations 101’

The internal documents also contain training materials for Amazon’s Canadian managers, which can help them spot “employee relations events” for inclusion in Atlas.

Titled Employee Relations 101, the materials set out how “leaders” should approach employees in a range of situations and circumstances, including to stave off what Amazon views as the threat of unionisation.

“Overall, a union coming into your site could fundamentally change the way it operates today. It would likely add layers of bureaucracy and jeopardize your ability to make changes to improve the workplace for employees as well as improve the end customer experience,” one document states.

“It is important then for you to recognize and escalate labor activity concerns quickly. This will help ensure we are doing all we can to build trust, minimize disruptions, and maintain safe operations.”

Elsewhere in the documents, Amazon adds: “Whether internally started or externally started – strategy of unions is like strategy of someone splitting wood. Look for a crack and put a wedge there to drive separation between management and employees.”

Amazon then goes on to highlight a range of indicators that could signal possible union activity, urging managers to get in touch with its HR and employee relations departments if they, for example, notice an abnormal increase in absenteeism, or groups of employees start asking increasingly hostile questions about company benefits and policies.

It also highlights employees starting to use expressions related to labour discussions, including “grievance”, “just cause”, “living wage”, or “seniority” as something to watch out for, or using phrases common in labour organising like “we” and “on behalf of”.

It added that other signs of “escalating labor activity” include third-party flyers, anti-Amazon or union graffiti, and lists of demands circulating where people raise concerns on behalf of co-workers.

The presentation also trains managers on how to deal with employees in ways that do not violate their labour rights when signs of union activity are spotted.

Using the acronym “FORE”, it notes that managers “can have open, two-way conversations that avoid violating employee rights by focusing on sharing facts, opinions, rules and experiences”.

This section adds that while “you can always remind employees of the benefits they have as an employee with Amazon” – including competitive pay, a “comprehensive” benefits package and career growth opportunities – “sharing negative opinions and experiences about unions [or unionisation] is a high-risk activity … [because it] is not permitted employer speech” in certain Canadian provinces.

In terms of VOA use – one of the key communication channels that feeds into Amazon’s Atlas system – it advises managers not to use security cameras to determine who wrote a comment on the electronic bulletin, and specifically says “do not discipline employees for VOA comments without approval from Legal”.

The document goes on to instruct managers to follow another acronym, TIPS, which reminds them to never “threaten, interrogate, promise or spy”.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s request for comment on why it sees workers organising as a threat to its business, an Amazon spokesperson said its employees always have the option of joining a union or not, and that what matters most to the company is the direct relationships between workers and managers.

They added that any mention of maintaining operations or minimising disruption made in the documents refers to when there is industrial action, should it happen.

An Amazon spokesperson informed Computer Weekly that the system referred to in the documents is no longer called Atlas, but declined to divulge what the system is currently named.

In April 2020, Computer Weekly reported that Amazon-owned Whole Foods was using an interactive “heat-mapping” tool to track dozens of metrics – such as employee turnover, diversity and proximity to union offices – to predict and mitigate unionisation risks at its 510 US stores.

title: Starling Bank claims first banking AI trained on UK sovereign cloud
raw_text:
Starling Bank has laid claim to be the first bank to train an artificial intelligence (AI) model on a UK sovereign cloud, after it announced it would develop its own transactional foundation model (TFM) with Nvidia and train it on Civo’s UK cloud infrastructure.

The TFM will train on more than 15 billion anonymised transactions and other events from Starling’s own systems, and in time will form a single Starling Intelligence layer underpinning the bank’s AI capabilities. It is due in production in early 2027, first to sharpen fraud detection and then to improve Starling Assistant, the bank’s agentic AI financial assistant.

Sebastian Khan, data scientist and technical lead on the TFM at Starling, said the model differs from an off-the-shelf large language model (LLM) because it is “tailor-made to crunch and understand transactions”. Where an LLM learns the meaning of a word from the sentence around it, he said, a TFM learns what a transaction represents from the events around it.

“Let’s say you have a regular morning coffee in your hometown at 9am every day, but maybe you go on holiday, and you have a morning coffee at 9am while you’re away,” he said. “It’s the same coffee transaction for the same-ish price, but the transactions surrounding it are probably going to be quite different.”

Khan said the model is Starling’s own IP, developed “from the ground up completely in-house” but “standing on the shoulders of giants”, including Revolut’s Pragma model, Visa’s Transaction GPTs research and Nvidia’s financial-services blueprints.

The model trains on tokenised data. Khan said Starling does not use personally identifiable information, and that tokenisation is itself a form of anonymisation, with raw values such as a postcode replaced by an integer embedded into a vector space.

“We keep separate the tokeniser, which is basically the map from the raw to the encoded data,” he said. “Even if someone was to get access to the encoded data, there would be no way of decoding it without the tokeniser.”

That tokenisation happens not on Civo’s UK infrastructure but in Starling’s existing Google Cloud environment, where the bank’s data warehouse lives. Khan said this carried no additional data sovereignty risk. “There’s no elevated risk,” he said. “It’s sort of standard business practice.”

The move forms part of a multicloud strategy, said Mark Boost, chief executive of Civo. “Everyone, to some degree, should live in a multicloud strategy, because they shouldn’t necessarily be locked into a single provider,” he added. “We just want to be one of those cloud providers in a multicloud strategy.”

Starling, he said, was “keen to back a British provider”, and the UK should “be less of a taker and more of a maker, as Keir Starmer said last year”. The move also echoes the UK government’s financial services AI adoption plan, co-authored by Starling group CIO Harriet Rees, a UK government AI champion for financial services, which flags the sector’s reliance on a small number of global cloud and AI providers.

Where the sovereignty line is drawn is the most contested part of the announcement, and Boost’s framing is one of control. “The most important question is, can someone turn it off? Is there a digital kill switch?” he said. “These are silicon chips that sit in a datacentre in the UK, and Nvidia can’t turn it off as such.”

The real limits of data sovereignty

The claim that a model is “sovereign” because it runs on a UK cloud provider in a UK datacentre rests on a narrower definition of sovereignty than many recognise.

Computer Weekly’s reporting on cloud sovereignty found that many such claims rest on corporate policy and marketing rather than verifiable technical mechanisms. The decisive question is not where the servers sit, but whose jurisdiction can reach them.

Under the US Cloud Act and FISA Section 702, US authorities can compel US companies to hand over data regardless of where it is stored. Under 18 USC 2705(b), courts can attach non-disclosure orders – gag orders – to those demands, forbidding the provider from telling its customer anything has happened.

That matters for two reasons. First, Starling tokenises its data on Google Cloud, a US hyperscaler, before it ever reaches Civo. Second, the model runs on Nvidia silicon and Nvidia’s software stack, updated from the US. A global supply chain where code is authored and signed at a US headquarters makes the routine software update a potential invisible vector for state-level intervention.

There is also the question of the model itself. A growing body of argument holds that a trained model encodes statistical representations of its training data, so sovereignty must be treated as an end-to-end chain – the raw data, the training pipeline, the model weights, the inference outputs and the derived insights. A single weak link breaks the chain, and transformation such as tokenisation does not strip jurisdiction.

None of this makes Starling’s move worthless. Training on a UK-owned cloud reduces dependence on a handful of US hyperscalers and builds domestic capability. But “sovereign cloud” and “all data within UK jurisdiction only” describe a step along a journey rather than a destination.

The argument from Starling and Civo is that sovereignty comes from the cloud provider rather than the silicon. So, because Civo is UK-owned and its datacentres sit in the UK, the data sits only under UK jurisdiction.

But that leaves Nvidia, a US company, supplying both the hardware and much of the software stack, with the CUDA ecosystem updated from the US.

Boost acknowledged the supply-chain reality: “In a perfect world, every single thing is kept in the UK, built in the UK. But realistically, the top chips are being made by American companies right now – they’re the top performing – there’s not a lot of choice elsewhere.”

As Computer Weekly reported on the limits of data sovereignty, US authorities can reach data held by US companies wherever it sits. 

Khan said the bank was “about to start training on real data in Civo”, having spent several months building the codebase in-house, and was first testing the pipeline – a Kubeflow pipeline on Civo – with synthetic data. The target is more than 15 billion events, “but that figure is preliminary”.

The first planned use case is fraud detection, where existing models rely on what Khan called “traditional feature engineering, which is sort of a dark art”. A model that captures sequential information could deliver “a boost in fraud detection”, he said, before work turns to Starling Assistant. How often the model will need retraining remains open.

“I’m actually an expert in drift detection, so knowing when training data and model predictions start to become out of date,” Khan said.

title: Microsoft CVE volumes on relentless upward trajectory
raw_text:
Aided in large part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday update has once again addressed a record number of common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs), with over 1,400 flaws listed, mor than in the entirety of 2023.

This blows past the previous record of approximately 1,000 set one month ago, which in turn superseded that of a little over 600 set in July 2026. By way of comparison, the October 2025 update addressed roughly 175 CVEs. It is important to note that exact totals often vary and are hard to pin down thanks to the presence of third-party flaws and how they are counted.

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative, conceded that he was starting to think he doesn’t much care for the new normal as he described a “breaking point” for enterprise patch management.

When AI can generate essentially a year’s worth of vulnerabilities in 30 days, any organisations still cleaving to traditional monthly triage patch management models are leaving their network boundaries dangerously exposed, he explained.

“Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly,” said Childs.

“It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding – and fixing – more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.

“The volume isn’t the real story anymore,” he told Computer Weekly via email. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what’s proven, prioritised, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.”

This month, Childs noted in particular the presence of 55 unauthenticated, zero-click vulnerabilities across DHCP, Remote Desktop Gateway, and Network Policy Server – mass wormable attack surfaces that create the “highest lateral propagation risk in years.”

High-profile flaws

Diving into some of the more high-profile flaws listed this month, Childs advised defenders to prioritise immediate perimeter ring-fencing to counter an active zero-day command injection in Windows Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-96951, that bypasses Mark of the Web (MotW) protections. This flaw was supposedly discovered in part by Anthropic’s Claude AI model and has already made it to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (Cisa’s) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (Kev) catalogue.

Also worth close attention, he said, is CVE-2026-102866, an elevation of privilege (EoP) flaw in SharePoint that enables an unauthenticated attacker to exploit a cryptographic token validation issue to take control of user accounts.

Action1 vulnerability research director Jack Bicer said that for security leaders, the challenge this month will not be in simply deploying more updates but in deciding what needs attention first without causing any issues for downstream services.

“This month, the answer depends on more than severity scores,” wrote Bicer. “Active exploitation, exposed services, and the role each system plays in your network should guide deployment order.”

Sick days for CISOs

Meanwhile, research conducted on behalf of Cardiff-based cyber security consultancy Socura has reported that Patch Tuesday causes major stress among cyber professionals, with nearly a third feeling “significant anxiety” in the days running up to the second Tuesday of the month, and a fifth saying that they had either deliberately called in sick or planned holiday time specifically to avoid having to deal with it.

“You expect your accountant to be available for your tax return deadline, and your lawyer for your court date,” said Andrew Kays, Socura CEO.

“It speaks volumes about the unhealthy levels of stress and burnout in our industry that cyber security leaders would deliberately avoid the office during their most consequential day of work. CVE numbers are rising every year and with AI facilitating cyber criminals to exploit vulnerabilities faster than ever, I think Patch Tuesday stress could get worse before it gets better.

“Fortunately, while AI is making Patch Tuesday more difficult, the same AI tools and resources are also in the hands of defenders. AI is improving our customer outcomes, and the time it takes to respond to an incident. And this is the case for many security teams,” he said.

title: Journalists subject to unlawful surveillance seek legal costs after ‘unreasonable conduct’ by PSNI
raw_text:
Two Belfast journalists who were placed under unlawful police surveillance are seeking costs following allegations of “unreasonable behaviour” by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) during legal proceedings.

Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney argue that they should be awarded compensation to cover wasted costs for two abandoned court hearings, after the PSNI failed to properly disclose evidence at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

The case, heard at the Court of Appeal in London, before Lord Justices Bean, Edis, and Lewis, will decide whether the UK’s most secret court has legal powers to make awards for legal costs to victims of unlawful surveillance.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal awarded the two journalists damages of £4,000 each in December 2025 after finding they had been unlawfully spied on by the PSNI and the Metropolitan Police, including monitoring phone data, in an attempt to identify their confidential sources.

The three appeal court judges decided on 13 October 2026 that they could hear an appeal from the journalists to challenge the IPT’s conclusion, overturning arguments from the PSNI that the case was a matter for a judicial review.

The case follows a ruling by five tribunal judges in April 2025 that they had no statutory powers to award legal costs to Birney and McCaffrey for hearings that had to be postponed because of the PSNI’s conduct.

Ben Jaffey KC told the court that the Investigatory Powers Tribunal erred in law by finding it had no jurisdiction to award costs to Birney and McCaffrey. The tribunal was also wrong to conclude that it would not be “just and appropriate” to increase the compensation awarded to the journalists to reflect their legal costs, he said.

“Should the tribunal’s determination be allowed to stand, the consequences would be startling. Awarding costs to address improper conduct is an essential tool to control judicial proceedings,” Jaffey argued in written submissions. “The PSNI’s approach to disclosure could well have led to a significant miscarriage of justice.”

Unlawful arrests

In 2028, Birney and McCaffrey were unlawfully arrested, had their homes and business premises searched, and computer equipment seized by Northern Ireland police, in the wake of their documentary No Stone Unturned, which exposed collusion between the police and a paramilitary group.

They were vindicated by the High Court in Northern Ireland in 2019, which found that the PSNI’s conduct in applying for search warrants “fell woefully short of the standards required” and that there was no “overriding requirement in the public interest” that could have interfered with the protection of journalistic sources.

In the same year, they brought a case to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal against the PSNI, MI5, GCHQ, the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police and others, alleging unlawful surveillance.

Jaffey said in legal submissions that the PSNI “derailed” a substantive hearing in February 2024 after the police force disclosed the existence of a directed surveillance order against the journalists two days before the case was due to start.

“It appears that, until this point, the PSNI was intent on keeping the authorisation secret from the applicants,” he said in written submissions.

At the same time, the PSNI disclosed that it had received and used extensive unlawfully obtained communications data from the Metropolitan Police.

“If this material had not been disclosed at the last moment, it is likely that there would have been a miscarriage of justice: the Metropolitan Police’s unlawful conduct would have gone entirely undiscovered,” Jaffey stated. “The ultimate but predictable effect of this conduct was to derail the substantive hearing.”

There were similar problems at a follow-on hearing in May 2024, when large volumes of material were belatedly disclosed, requiring extensive further work by lawyers for the journalists.

“The PSNI had consistently provided key material at the eleventh hour – and, even then, had done so reluctantly and by way of dumping large quantities of documents,” Jaffey argued.

This meant that lawyers had to parse the documents overnight on the eve of a hearing. “Had the appellants not had the benefit of legal representation, key material would never have been put before the tribunal and it is unlikely that justice would have been done,” Jaffey stated.

Parliament did not give IPT powers to award costs

Acting for the PSNI, Cathryn McGahey KC said that there was nothing in legislation to confer jurisdiction for costs for the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

“If Parliament wanted to confer a cost regime, it would have done so,” she said.

She said that the IPT found that it was not appropriate to increase the compensation awarded to McCaffrey and Birney in this case to reflect the additional costs incurred. The applicants were saying they accepted that the IPT was a “cost-free regime” unless there were exceptional circumstances, she said, and in this case were seeking costs for two wasted court hearings.

Lord Justice Lewis said that, on that reading, the journalists had been foolish as they could have asked for all their costs.

McGahey told the court that the tribunal makes a broad award for damages “which is never going to reflect the costs of people represented”, adding:  “There is no reason to revisit the award already made when it reflects conduct that the tribunal [was] already aware of.”

The court has reserved judgment.

How the PSNI delayed disclosure of key evidence

16 February 2024: Durham Police incorrectly told the lawyers of the journalists there had been no Directed Surveillance Authorisation against them.

16 February 2024: PSNI served a “skeleton argument” making additional disclosures but neglected to disclose the Directed Surveillance Authorisation.

23 February 2024: PSNI disclosed the existence of a Directed Surveillance Authorisation issued to authorise spying against the journalists “only two clear days” before a court hearing: “No clear explanation has ever been offered for that exceptionally late disclosure.”

25 February 2024: PSNI discloses further evidence at 11:19pm on the evening before a court hearing.

26 February 2024: On the day of the scheduled court hearing, a lawyer for the two journalists was allowed to view and take limited notes of the Directed Surveillance Authorisation only the morning before the court hearing.

Lawyers for the journalists attempt to make sense of large volumes of additional material disclosed just before the court hearing. This includes a disclosure from the PSNI that it had received extensive phone communications data from the Metropolitan Police Service, which was later added as a respondent to the case.

The hearing is adjourned late on the first day as it could “not fairly go ahead”.

8 May 2024: PSNI discloses large volumes of evidence raising new issues, including a “defensive operation” to monitor police phone calls to journalists by the PSNI, and details of an attempt by a Durham Constabulary to preserve journalist Trevor Birney’s emails stored on Apple’s iCloud. The tribunal ordered further searches of evidence and written explanations for the late disclosure.

title: NCA cracks down on foreign cyber fraudsters
raw_text:
The UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) has hosted a major operation targeting cyber fraud and scams originating from across Africa, culminating in almost 30 arrests – principally in Ghana and Nigeria – and the removal and closure of 3.7 million online profiles and accounts.

More than 100 law enforcement personnel from overseas agencies – including members of the Five Eyes Law Enforcement Group (FELEG) such as the FBI – along with the Nigerian Police Force and Ghana’s Cyber Security Authority convened in London to participate in the “operational intensification” targeting organised cyber criminals and their infrastructure.

The three-day operation culminated in a series of on-the-ground actions targeting individuals who use fake social media profiles to carry out investment and impersonation fraud, among other things. Industry representatives from the likes of Google and Meta also joined in, working with Report Fraud to provide a stream of data identifying their targets.

“Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it,” said NCA deputy director of fraud, Nick Sharp.

“Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilise the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud.

“Fraudsters can operate from anywhere and will target victims both domestically and globally. The NCA will continue to work with international and private sector partners to tackle fraudsters working upstream, overseas and online.

“Collaborating in this way sends a clear signal to criminals that the combined capabilities of law enforcement and industry means that we will relentlessly pursue them and the infrastructure they rely on no matter where they operate,” he said.

Jeanine Pirro, US attorney for the District of Columbia (DC) and founder of the Scam Center Strike Force, added: “Transnational fraud demands a transnational response. I have partnered with the NCA and the Crown Prosecutor for England and Wales to push forward cases on both sides of the Atlantic; criminals are not hindered by borders and neither are we. We will deploy our team wherever in the world transnational criminals target innocent victims.”

Results delivered

Some of the more notable success stories to emerge from the operation include the arrests of 19 people and the seizure of 303 electronic devices in the town of Sasaabi, outside the Ghanaian capital Accra. A total of 117 people were also identified as victims of human trafficking and are now set to return to their homes.

Ghanaian police also led a series of raids on scam centres in the Sasaabi area at the end of September, resulting in additional arrests and property seizures. A number of people taken into custody were also identified as having been forced into criminal activity after being abducted and trafficked.

Meanwhile, in Nigeria’s oil-rich Delta State, nine arrests were made alongside the seizure of six laptops, 35 smartphones and 12 routers.

In addition to the suspension of 3.7 million fake accounts and profiles by Meta, a total of $11m in potential freezable funds were identified by the private sector participants.

Investment fraud

Investment fraud such as that allegedly perpetrated by those arrested is a widespread form of fraud that lures people with promises of guaranteed returns for low- or no-risk investments that turn out to be nothing of the kind. Often, they target investment opportunities in areas such as digital assets and cryptocurrency, Ponzi and pyramid schemes, or property.

Investment fraudsters will use a range of tactics to fool their targets, such as presenting endorsements from well-known figures, inviting them to join exclusive investment groups, and high-pressure tactics such as creating a sense of urgency with time-limited special offers. Such schemes are often carefully concocted to drip feed some small returns to the unsuspecting victim to convince them they are legitimate.

Frequently, victims will also be coerced into handing over more money than their initial ‘investment’ in the form of supposed ‘taxes’ or ‘handling fees’ required to ‘unlock’ their money.

More information on how investment fraud works can be found at the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Centre (IC3), and more general cyber fraud protection advice is available from the National Cyber Security Centre. If you are located in the UK and believe you have been a victim of investment fraud, you can also report it to Report Fraud in confidence.

title: Government could firm up pension insourcing position next month
raw_text:
The Civil Service union has claimed insourcing government pension schemes could deliver “immediate improvements”, and said the government’s strategic review should not be used to delay change.

In a briefing sent to Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union members, the union said the government’s Strategic Review of Pension Scheme Delivery, described as being at “discovery phase”, is considering a range of options, including insourcing and increased digital delivery for Capita's botched Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) and Royal Mail Statutory Pension Scheme.

The CSPS is administered by Capita, but is beset with huge delays in paying civil servants' pensions. The Royal Mail pension was run by Capita before its contract was terminated in April after failing to hit important milestones.

title: IMF warns of cyber threat to digitally connected financial markets
raw_text:
The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 Global financial stability report has highlighted the risk financial institutes face as they become digital and interconnected. In the report, the IMF warned that this interconnectivity leads to a greater risk of cyber disruptions which has emerged as a growing source of systemic risk. 

The IMF noted that cyber threats constitute a growing systemic risk as financial services become more digital and interconnected, stating that frontier AI models are emerging as both powerful enablers of cyber attacks and critical defensive tools.

“A major attack affecting payments, trading or access to deposits could cause immediate losses and undermine confidence,” the report’s authors warned.

In the report, the IMF noted that rapid digitisation has expanded the attack surface. First is the exposure to disruption due to the fact that financial institutions increasingly depend on interconnected technologies, cloud services, third-party providers, and real-time payment and settlement systems.

The second risk identified in the IMF report is that there is growing reliance on a small number of critical technology providers, together with increasingly complex and often opaque third-party dependency chains. The report’s authors warned that this supply chain increases concentration risk and creates potential common points of failure across financial institutions.

The third is the growing sophistication of cyber threats. “State-sponsored actors, ransomware groups and insiders now have access to increasingly powerful tools, including frontier AI models that have demonstrated strong capabilities in network-attack simulations,” the IMF warned. These developments are making cyber defence more challenging.

It noted that the number of reported vulnerabilities has risen sharply as the time between the disclosure and exploitation of vulnerabilities has been reduced significantly. In over 70% of cases in 2026, the IMF said that software providers had almost no time to patch vulnerabilities before exploitation began, a jump of 20% compared to a year ago.

While the report’s authors note that AI can help to address shortages of cyber expertise through stronger monitoring, threat detection and automated response to cyber attacks, AI also increases the urgency of strengthening foundational cyber resilience, including cyber hygiene, incident reporting, crisis preparedness and oversight of critical third-party providers.

Responding to a question about the cyber threat to financial institutes and the global financial market, Caio Ferreira, deputy division chief in the global markets analysis division at the IMF, said that all countries need to address the risks identified by the IMF: “Which regions become more vulnerable in this sense are those that do not have appropriate prevention, and what we see globally is that prevention has been challenged by a lack of availability of cyber security professionals.”

Ferreira referenced data showing that there is a 40% shortfall in the number people needed in cyber security. Looking at specific regions, he said: “I think that broadly we see emerging markets as being less prepared but cyber threats impact every country. In advanced economies, it’s important to improve the focus on understanding what are the main nodes that can impact the cyber threats and the operational connections between different parts of the financial sector.”

title: Infosys boss describes AI job fears as ‘hogwash’
raw_text:
The boss of Indian IT services giant Infosys has said fears over artificial intelligence (AI) taking jobs is ”hogwash”, stating that the technology will fuel demand for new human skills.

Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Infosys chairman Nandan Nilekani stressed the need for people to provide the skills needed for AI to deliver.

According to a Bloomberg report, he said: “Business transformation is not just about coding. Seventy percent is governance, change management, transformation, guardrails.

Nilekani asked: “How do you make sure AI bots don’t hallucinate? How do you make sure agents don’t go rogue?”

The need for people is “more than ever before” for companies like Infosys, he added.

Nilekani said there will be new jobs understanding customer needs, collaborating, and getting people to work together.

Companies such as Infosys grew through offering IT skills to Western countries from India at a fraction of the cost of the same skills in Europe and the US. But today, the companies have established themselves on the top table when it comes to customer portfolios and the breadth of services they offer.

While AI can now complete a significant chunk of coding requirements, Nilekani said that accounts for just a fraction in any services project. He added that fears of AI fuelling job losses is the result of “disaster marketing to suit the interests of large capital”.

But for how long?

Sam Kingston, CEO of software services company Zenitech and former UK head of EDS’s UK private sector business, said Nilekani’s argument “won’t hold”.

“I agree to a point, but then it will drop and it won’t create jobs,” he said. “It will actually make people more efficient, and that then means that the speed of delivery is faster, and you’ll also use less people, senior and qualified people, to do that.”

Kingston said mid and junior level workers will be hit in the beginning as seniors will be doing work alongside AI.

There will be a diminishing correlation between business growth and workforce growth at IT services firms. Traditionally, more people were required as more business was won, but AI is changing this.

Hexaware, a Tier 2 Indian firm with thousands of staff, presents an example of how things are changing. Amrinder Singh, head of EMEA at Hexaware, told Computer Weekly last year that the company has a self-imposed target for AI delivery. “One of the vision statements we have is that by 2030, we want nearly 50% of our work to be delivered, and revenue generated, through digital labour, not just human labour,” he said.

This, added Singh, does not mean the human workforce will be smaller. On the contrary, with the growth of the industry fuelled by AI projects, more staff will be needed. But he admitted the growth of the human workforce may slow down.

Singh voiced a warning: “There is no future for single-skilled people. Unless you are multi-skilled with domain understanding, as well as an understanding of how to use AI and technology, you will not survive,” he said.

Like workers in business roles, tech staff must retrain for a world with AI if they are to prosper.
